place.zh: 银叶谷 · 石洞 · 夜
place.en: The Silver-leaf Vale · a cave · night

setup.zh: 崖壁下一个浅石洞。你生起一小堆火挡在洞口，怀里是阿禾的鸡蛋和娘烙的那张厚饼。
setup.en: A shallow cave under the cliff. You light a small fire across the mouth; inside your jacket, Ahe's egg and the thick flatbread your mother made.

recap.zh: 石洞里生了火，你把吃的分给它，给它擦伤口；睡着前，有人说：本王记住你了。
recap.en: In the cave you lit a fire, shared your food with the fox and cleaned its wounds; as you fell asleep someone said: this king will remember you.

zh: 怀里两样东西：一个剥了壳的鸡蛋，一张厚饼。
en: A shallow cave, a small fire.
The resin crackles; no beast comes near.
Two things in your jacket: a peeled egg, a thick flatbread.

story.zh:
他在崖壁底下找到了一个浅浅的石洞，先往里扔了一块石头，听了听，是空的；又扔了一块，又听了听，还是空的；待要再捡第三块，想想算了，还是进去了。

他用他爹教的法子，拿那把火镰敲着火石，引着了干苔和松脂，生了一小堆火，火堆挡在洞口，野兽便不敢进来。

然后他从怀里摸出了两样东西：阿禾给的那个鸡蛋，已经剥了壳，锁儿闻过的；和他娘给的那张厚饼——沈家最后的一点白面。
story.en:
At the cliff foot he found a shallow cave. First he tossed a stone in and listened — empty. He tossed another and listened again — still empty. He was about to pick up a third, then thought better of it and went in.

By the method his father had taught him he struck the fire-steel on the flint, caught the dry moss and pine resin, and made a small fire; a fire across the cave mouth keeps the beasts out.

Then he took two things from his jacket: Ahe's egg, already peeled, the one Suo'er had smelled; and the thick flatbread his mother had given him — the last of the Shens' white flour.

exits.means: shares the egg and the bread with the fox, feeds it

story.zh:
他捏着那个鸡蛋，捏了半晌，才掰了一半，放在它嘴边，它闻了闻，看了他一眼，吃了。他想了一想，把另一半也放在它嘴边，它闻了闻，又看了他一眼，又吃了。

跟着是饼。他把饼掰成两半，一半给它，一半自己拿着。他饿了一整天，那半张饼在他手里，重得像一块金子。它把它那一半吃完了，便看着他手里这一半，又看了他一眼。他看着它，它看着他，火堆「噼啪」响了一声。

他把自己那一半掰下一大块来，放在它嘴边，剩下一个小角包好了，塞进包袱最底下，留作明天的早饭。它吃完了，舔了舔嘴，把脑袋一扭，闭上了眼睛，连个谢字也没有。

他撕下一片衣摆，蘸着雨水，一点一点地给它擦伤口上的泥。它不咬他了，只是在他碰到疼处时，耳朵往后一压，小小地「呜」一声。火光里，他瞧见它的伤口正在慢慢地、慢慢地合拢。

伤口是合拢了，天黑透了没多久，它却发起烧来。隔着那件旧外衣，一股热气一阵一阵地透将出来，烫得他手心发汗。他把衣裳掀开一角，只见它蜷得更紧了，鼻头干得起了皮，喘气又短又急，一口气到了喉咙口便折回来，像一只拉破了的风箱。

他爹说过，山里的活物受了重伤，头一夜总要发烧，熬过去就活，熬不过去就不活。

这句话他记得很清楚，因为他爹说完了，又补了一句：「人也一样。」

他没有药，只有雨水。他把那片衣摆撕成两块，一块蘸湿了搭在它脑门上，另一块伸到洞口去接雨，等这一块捂热了，便换那一块。守火的人不能睡，睡着了，火就灭了。想来想去，只有一个法子能叫自己不睡着，便是说话。

洞里没有别人，只有一只狐狸，那便跟它说。他自己浑身也是湿的，外衣又裹在它身上，冷得牙齿直打架，便把身子往火边挪了又挪。

他本想先告诉它自己叫什么，想了一想，一只狐狸，记住了也没处写，便省了。崖根底下那个孩子，他也没有说。他跟它说他娘那十七个盆，说他爹那只会聊天的膝盖，说后天就是立冬，马三要来拿他爷爷的弓，还说那叫传承。

说到马小宝，他道：「他手里永远捏着一块桂花糕。桂花糕是什么味儿，我到现在都不知道。闻着是香的。你吃过吗？——哦，你是狐狸，你吃鸡。」说到桂花糕的时候，它的耳朵动了一下。他只当是烧得难受，一只狐狸，哪里听得懂人话。

他又跟它说那只碗，在半空里翻了两个筋斗，他伸手去捞，差了一寸。

「我家的人都这样，」他说，「谁疼了，都不说疼。我爹的膝盖疼，他说它在聊天；我娘蹲在地上捡碗，她什么都不说；我摔成这样，我也不说。我家的规矩，疼了不说，也没人问。问了，就得答；答了，就得哭；哭了，饭就凉了。」

说完这几句，他起身换了一回布，它身上还是烫的。

到了半夜，火堆矮了下去。他猫着腰钻出洞去，摸到崖根底下折了几根枯枝，每折一根，满树的银叶子便「叮叮」地响成一片，好像在骂人。

他只得小声道：「对不住，借两根。明儿还你。」他抱着柴，竖起耳朵往崖上听，只听见雨，别的什么也听不见。他爹的耳朵，听得见三里外的獐子；他的耳朵，只是一般。

他抱着柴钻回洞里，把火重新拨旺，一回头，却见它躺在那里，一动不动了。

他脑子里「嗡」的一声，扑过去把它捧了起来。它身上还烫着，可胸口那一起一伏，他瞧了半天，竟瞧不出来。他把耳朵贴到它身上听，什么也听不见，只听见自己的心在怦怦乱跳。

他捧着它，手足无措，平日里一张嘴能说会道，这时候翻来覆去，只说得出一句：「喂。喂。你别——」说到这里，不知怎的，他又算起账来，一面算，一面冲它嚷：「你吃了我家最后的白面！你吃了阿禾的鸡蛋！你咬了我一口！你这一死，这几笔账，我找谁要去？」

他嚷完了，洞里静悄悄的，只有火「噼啪」响了一声。过了好一会儿——也许只有一口气那么长，他却觉得比一整夜还长——它的胸口，轻轻地，鼓了一下。又鼓了一下。他捧着它坐倒在地下，半天说不出话来，后背上全是冷汗。

从那以后，他便不敢停嘴了，倒像他一停，它那口气便也要跟着停。

他把这十二年的事翻来覆去说了个遍，说到后来，自己也不知道在说些什么，只是嘴不停，手也不停，换布，添柴，再换布，再添柴。快到天亮的时候，雨停了。

他伸手去摸它，它身上不烫了，喘气也匀了，一下一下，又长又稳，跟坑里那一点银光一明一暗的样子一模一样。

他实在太累了，抱着它靠在石壁上，不知什么时候便睡着了。睡着之前，他好像听见有人在他耳边，用很小很小的声音说了一句话——不是狐狸叫，是人话，是一个姑娘的声音，带着几分不情不愿：⟪「……凡人。本王记住你了。」⟫
story.en:
He held the egg and stopped a moment. Then he broke it in half and set one half by its mouth; it sniffed, gave him a look, and ate. He thought a moment and set the other half by its mouth too; it sniffed, gave him another look, and ate that too.

Then the flatbread. He broke it in two, gave it half, and kept half. He'd been hungry all day; that half in his hand weighed like a lump of gold. It finished its half and looked at his, then at him. He looked at it; it looked at him; the fire crackled. He broke a big piece off his own half and set it by its mouth, wrapped the little corner left over and tucked it at the bottom of his bundle, for tomorrow's breakfast.

It finished, licked its lips, turned its head away and shut its eyes — not so much as a thank-you.

He tore a strip from his hem, wet it with rainwater, and bit by bit wiped the mud from its wounds. It didn't bite him any more; only when he touched a sore place its ears went flat and it gave a small *whuu*. In the firelight he saw its wounds closing, slowly, slowly.

The wounds had closed; but not long after full dark it began to burn with fever. Through the old jacket, heat came off it in waves, making his palms sweat. He lifted a corner: it was curled tighter than ever, its nose dry and peeling, its breath short and fast, each one turning back at the throat, like a torn bellows.

His father had said: a creature badly hurt in the mountains always runs a fever the first night; get through it and it lives, don't and it doesn't.

He remembered this very clearly, because his father had added: "People too."

He had no medicine, only rainwater. He tore the strip of hem in two, wetted one and laid it on its forehead, and held the other out of the cave mouth to catch the rain; when one grew warm, he swapped it for the other. Whoever keeps the fire mustn't sleep; fall asleep, and the fire goes out. He thought and thought, and there was only one way to keep himself awake: talking.

There was no one else in the cave, only a fox — so he talked to it. He was soaked through himself, his jacket wrapped round the fox, his teeth chattering, and he shifted closer and closer to the fire.

He'd meant to tell it his name first, then thought: a fox — even if it remembered, it had nowhere to write it down — and skipped that. The child at the foot of the cliff he didn't tell it about either. He told it about his mother's seventeen basins, about his father's chatty knee, about the Start of Winter being the day after tomorrow, when Ma San would come for his grandpa's bow, and call that inheritance.

When he got to Ma Xiaobao, he said, "He's always got a piece of osmanthus cake in his hand. What osmanthus cake tastes like, I still don't know. It smells good. Have you ever had any? — Oh, you're a fox, you eat chickens." When he mentioned the osmanthus cake, its ear twitched. He took it for the fever; a fox couldn't understand human talk.

He told it about the bowl, too: two somersaults in the air, and he'd grabbed for it and been an inch short.

"We're all like that in my family," he said. "Whoever's hurting doesn't say. My dad's knee hurts, he says it's chatting; my mum crouches picking up the bowl and says nothing; I'm smashed up like this and I don't say either. Our family's rule: when it hurts you don't say, and nobody asks. Ask, and you have to answer; answer, and you'll cry; cry, and the food goes cold."

When he'd said this much he got up and changed the cloth again. It was still burning.

In the middle of the night the fire burned low. He stooped out of the cave and felt his way to the foot of the cliff to break off a few dead branches; every one he snapped set the whole tree's silver leaves jingling, *ding-ding*, as if it were scolding him.

All he could do was whisper, "Sorry, just borrowing two. I'll give them back tomorrow." Holding the wood, he pricked up his ears toward the clifftop and heard only rain, nothing else. His father's ears could hear a river deer three li away; his were only ordinary.

He crawled back into the cave with the wood, stirred the fire up again, turned — and saw it lying there, not moving.

His head went *hum*. He threw himself down and scooped it up. It was still hot, but the rise and fall of its chest — he stared and stared and couldn't make it out. He pressed his ear to it and heard nothing, only his own heart hammering.

He held it, helpless; he who could talk rings round anyone could only say, over and over, "Hey. Hey. Don't you —" and then somehow he was doing sums again, shouting at it as he did: "You ate my family's last white flour! You ate Ahe's egg! You bit me! You die now, and who do I collect these accounts from?"

When he'd shouted it the cave was silent, only the fire crackling once. After a good while — perhaps no longer than a single breath, though to him it felt longer than the whole night — its chest, gently, rose. And rose again. He sat down hard with it in his hands and couldn't speak for a long time, his back soaked in cold sweat.

From then on he didn't dare stop talking, as if, should he stop, its breath would stop with him.

He went through all twelve years of his life, over and over, until in the end he didn't know what he was saying; only his mouth didn't stop, and nor did his hands — change the cloth, add wood, change the cloth, add wood. Toward dawn the rain stopped.

He reached out and felt it: it wasn't hot any more, its breathing had evened out, long and steady, one breath after another, exactly like that silver light brightening and dimming in the pit.

He was too tired. Holding it, he leaned against the rock wall and at some point fell asleep. Just before he slept he seemed to hear someone speak in his ear, very, very softly — not a fox's cry, human words, a girl's voice, a little grudging: ⟪"…Mortal. This king will remember you."⟫

exits.means: keeps the food, eats it alone

story.zh:
小满把那个剥了壳的鸡蛋，自己吃了。饼，他掰下一大半，也塞进了嘴里；剩下一个小角，包好了，塞进包袱最底下，留作明天的早饭。

这不叫小气，这叫算账。他饿了一整天，明天还不知道有没有吃的。

它在他的衣裳里看着他，一直看着，没出声。他给看得有点心虚，撕下一片衣摆，蘸着雨水，一点一点地给它擦伤口上的泥。它不咬他了，只是在他碰到疼处时，耳朵往后一压。

他太累了，抱着它靠在石壁上，不知什么时候便睡着了。睡着之前，他好像听见有人在他耳边，用很小很小的声音说了一句话，是一个姑娘的声音，带着几分不情不愿：⟪「……凡人。小气。——本王记住你了。」⟫
story.en:
Xiaoman ate the peeled egg himself. The flatbread — he broke off the larger part and stuffed that in his mouth too; the little corner left over he wrapped and tucked at the bottom of his bundle, for tomorrow's breakfast.

That wasn't stinginess; that was keeping accounts. He'd been hungry all day, and tomorrow there might be nothing to eat at all.

Inside his jacket it watched him — kept watching, without a sound. The watching made him feel a little guilty; he tore a strip from his hem, wet it with rainwater, and bit by bit wiped the mud from its wounds. It didn't bite him any more; only when he touched a sore place its ears went flat.

He was too tired. Holding it, he leaned against the rock wall and at some point fell asleep. Just before he slept he seemed to hear someone speak in his ear, very, very softly — a girl's voice, a little grudging: ⟪"…Mortal. Stingy. — This king will remember you."⟫
